C005.subject: Dynamic comparative advantage
C005.object: welfare gains for developing economies under free trade when initial institutional quality is low
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Dynamic comparative advantage welfare gains for developing economies under free trade when initial institutional quality is low]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data on trade liberalization episodes and institutional quality indices (e.g., World Bank Doing Business, ICRG) to estimate heterogeneous welfare effects over time. — Directly tests whether countries with initially low institutional quality experience smaller welfare gains from trade liberalization, as predicted by the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic general equilibrium models incorporating institutional quality as a determinant of comparative advantage evolution (e.g., Acemoglu & Robinson-style frameworks with endogenous productivity growth). — Allows simulation of long-run welfare effects under varying initial institutional conditions to assess whether dynamic comparative advantage mechanisms reduce gains for low-institution settings.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on trade and institutions (e.g., from NBER, CEPR working paper series) focusing on developing economies. — Synthesizes conflicting evidence to determine the overall direction and confidence in the hypothesis, and identifies gaps for targeted empirical work.

C006.subject: Dynamic comparative advantage
C006.object: long-term welfare gains for developing economies under free trade
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Dynamic comparative advantage long-term welfare gains for developing economies under free trade]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of manufacturing export sophistication and productivity growth in East Asian vs. Sub-Saharan African economies post-2000 — Directly tests whether dynamic comparative advantage (e.g., moving up the value chain) is associated with long-term welfare gains or stagnation under free trade, comparing regions with different initial conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Survey of theoretical models on learning-by-exporting and path dependency in developing economies (e.g., Hausmann, Hwang, Rodrik 2007; Redding 1999) — Evaluates mechanisms by which dynamic comparative advantage could either lock countries into low-skill specialization or enable upgrading, providing predictions to be tested against the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of empirical studies on trade liberalization and long-run growth in developing economies (e.g., from World Bank or NBER working papers, 2000–2023) — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple countries and time periods to assess whether dynamic comparative advantage hinders or promotes welfare gains, identifying gaps and regional heterogeneity.

qualifier.geographic: East Asian and Sub-Saharan African developing economies

C007.subject: Infant industry protection
C007.object: greater long-run welfare gains than short-run losses for developing economies under free trade only when combined with domestic competition policy and export promotion
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Infant industry protection greater long-run welfare gains than short-run losses for developing economies under free trade only when combined with domestic competition policy and export promotion]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel studies of developing economies that implemented infant industry protections (e.g., South Korea, Brazil, India) with and without complementary competition and export policies, using measures like total factor productivity growth and export unit values over 20-30 year horizons. — Directly tests the conditional claim: comparing welfare outcomes across countries that combined protection with competition/export policies versus those that did not, controlling for initial conditions, isolates the interaction effect specified in the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic general equilibrium models with heterogeneous firms, learning-by-doing, and imperfect competition, calibrated to developing economy parameters, simulating the joint impact of temporary tariff protection, antitrust enforcement, and export subsidies on long-run consumer welfare. — Provides a rigorous causal framework to assess whether the hypothesized complementarities are theoretically necessary and sufficient for net long-run gains, identifying mechanisms and thresholds that empirical studies may miss.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of historical case studies from the 'East Asian Miracle' vs. Latin American import-substitution industrialization, focusing on the presence or absence of domestic competition policy and export promotion regimes. — Synthesizes existing qualitative and quantitative evidence to identify patterns of success and failure, offering a broader contextual test of the conditional hypothesis beyond single-country or single-sector analyses.

C008.subject: Infant industry protection
C008.object: long-term economic growth for developing economies under free trade
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Infant industry protection long-term economic growth for developing economies under free trade]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data analysis comparing long-term GDP growth rates of developing economies that implemented infant industry protection (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan) versus those that did not (e.g., many Sub-Saharan African countries), controlling for initial conditions and trade openness. — Provides direct quantitative evidence on whether protected industries eventually became competitive and contributed to sustained growth, or instead led to inefficiency and stagnation.

[PATH:empirical] Historical case studies of specific infant industries in East Asia (e.g., South Korea's steel industry) and Latin America (e.g., Brazil's computer industry) under protectionist policies, examining eventual export performance and productivity changes. — Allows nuanced causal inference about the conditions under which protection helps or hinders, addressing the disputed nature of the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of dynamic comparative advantage and learning-by-doing (e.g., Bardhan, 1970; Melitz, 2005) applied to developing economy settings, analyzing optimal tariff schedules and time horizons for protection. — Clarifies the mechanisms and necessary conditions (e.g., sufficient learning spillovers, limited capture) for infant industry protection to either promote or retard long-term growth, helping resolve conflicting empirical findings.

qualifier.geographic: developing economies in East Asia, Latin America, and Sub-Saharan Africa

C011.subject: Free trade policies
C011.predicate: produce a net welfare gain only if
C011.object: the rate of dynamic comparative advantage shift exceeds the rate of infant industry capital depreciation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies the rate of dynamic comparative advantage shift exceeds the rate of infant industry capital depreciation]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of trade liberalization episodes in developing economies (e.g., from World Bank or UNCTAD) comparing infant industry capital depreciation rates with subsequent dynamic comparative advantage shifts — Directly tests the core condition by quantifying both rates and their relationship to welfare outcomes in the specified geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models incorporating endogenous comparative advantage and capital depreciation in infant industries — Allows simulation of the threshold condition under rapid technological change, isolating welfare effects when the rate of comparative advantage shift exceeds capital depreciation.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of case studies on infant industry protection versus free trade in developing economies (e.g., East Asian vs. Latin American experiences) — Synthesizes historical evidence on whether welfare gains from free trade depend on the hypothesized rate differential, providing qualitative confirmation or refutation.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of rapid technological change
qualifier.geographic: in developing economies with significant infant industries

C012.subject: Protective trade policies
C012.object: long-term economic growth by preventing the natural development of competitive industries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Protective trade policies long-term economic growth by preventing the natural development of competitive industries]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of import substitution industrialization (ISI) in Latin America (e.g., Brazil, Argentina) versus export-oriented growth in East Asia (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan) during the 20th century — These contrasting policy regimes provide quasi-experimental evidence on whether protective trade policies stifle long-term growth by preventing competitive industry development, directly testing the hypothesis in the specified geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:empirical] Econometric analysis of tariff rates and total factor productivity growth in developing economies (e.g., using World Bank or IMF panel data from 1970-2020) — Quantitative estimation of the relationship between trade protection levels and productivity growth can isolate the hypothesized causal mechanism, controlling for other factors like institutional quality or human capital.

[PATH:theoretical] Literature review of infant industry argument studies (e.g., works by Ha-Joon Chang or Dani Rodrik) and critiques from classical trade theory (e.g., comparative advantage models) — A synthesis of theoretical arguments on whether temporary protection can foster competitive industries or instead entrench inefficiency will clarify the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions of the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: developing economies with nascent industrial sectors
